chapters.titleDe: Ser and estar, with subject pronouns
comic: Stop! For how you feel now, use estar.

blocks.text: Spanish has two verbs for “to be”: *ser* and *estar*. You need them to say who you are, where you are from, where you are and how you feel. Almost every first conversation uses them.

blocks.title: Why is this so important?
blocks.text: English has one verb here and Spanish has two, so you make this choice all the time. It can even change the meaning: *Es aburrido* = he is boring. *Está aburrido* = he is bored.
Subject pronouns and the two verbs

The verb ending already shows the person, so Spanish often drops the pronoun: *Soy Pablo. Estoy en Bilbao.* Use the pronoun for contrast or to be clear: *Yo soy de Vigo y ella es de Cádiz.* There is no pronoun for “it”: *Es grande.*

*Tú* is for friends, family, children and people your age. In Spain people use it a lot, also at work. *Usted* shows respect: if you are not sure at an office, start with it. It takes the same verb form as *él* and *ella*: *¿Usted es la doctora?* In Latin America people say *ustedes* instead of *vosotros*, also with friends.
ser: who or what someone or something is

head: Use
Example
rows: Soy Lucía. Este es mi hermano.
what someone or something is like
Javier es alto. El piso es pequeño.
Son las ocho. Hoy es lunes.

blocks.text: estar: where and how

head: Use
Example
rows: Estoy en casa. La farmacia está cerca.
La puerta está abierta. La sopa está fría.

blocks.text: A plain job needs no article after *ser*: *Soy enfermera*. With an adjective, use one: *Soy una enfermera muy buena.* Your age goes with *tener*, not *ser*: *Tengo 31 años.*

items: ¿De dónde eres? Soy de Senegal.
¿Dónde está el centro de salud? Está en la calle Mayor.
¿Cómo está usted? Muy bien, gracias.
Mis padres no están en casa. Están en el trabajo.

blocks.text: For the place of a person or a thing, use *estar*, never *ser*.

blocks.text: We use the present tense for habits and facts, for what is happening now, and often for the near future: *Vivo en Sevilla. Carmen trabaja de noche. Mañana trabajo por la tarde.*
The three groups: -ar, -er, -ir
Every Spanish verb ends in *-ar*, *-er* or *-ir* in the dictionary. Take off this ending and add the ending for the person.

The *-er* and *-ir* endings are the same, except with *nosotros* and *vosotros*: *comemos / vivimos*, *coméis / vivís*. The *vosotros* forms have a written accent. Stress is usually on the last syllable but one: *HA-blo, VI-ves*.
Common regular verbs
trabajar · estudiar · comprar · llamar · buscar · necesitar · beber · aprender · leer · escribir · abrir · recibir
How often? Words that often go with the present
siempre · normalmente · a menudo · a veces · casi nunca · nunca · todos los días · los lunes · los fines de semana
*Los lunes* means every Monday: *Los lunes trabajo en casa.* *El lunes* means this coming Monday: *El lunes tengo cita.* Spanish uses no word for “on” here.

items: ¿Dónde vives? Vivo en Zaragoza.
Nerea trabaja en una farmacia y estudia por las noches.
Mis hijos aprenden español en el colegio.
Los sábados compramos en el mercado.
¿Bebes café? Sí, todos los días.

blocks.text: The form with *-ar*, *-er* or *-ir* is only the dictionary form. In a sentence, the verb needs the ending for the person, and you usually don't need *yo*.

comic: Stop! No goes right before the verb.

blocks.text: Spanish needs no helping verb like “do” in questions and negatives. A question starts with ¿ and ends with ?, and your voice goes up. A negative usually needs only the word *no*.

blocks.title: Why is this so important?
blocks.text: Asking is how you get things done: at the town hall, at the doctor's, at the bank. With a few question words and *no*, you can ask for what you need and say what is not the case.
Yes/no questions
Take a normal sentence, write ¿ … ? around it and let your voice rise. The words don't have to change. The subject can also go after the verb: *¿Trabaja Lucía hoy?*

items: ¿Hablas inglés? Sí, un poco.
¿Usted vive aquí? No, vivo en Getafe.
¿Tienes cita? Sí, a las diez.

blocks.text: Question words

blocks.title: Question word + verb + subject
blocks.text: Question words always have a written accent. After the question word comes the verb, then the subject: *¿Dónde vive Javier?* (not *¿Dónde Javier vive?*). A preposition goes before the question word, never at the end: *¿De dónde eres? ¿Con quién vives?*

head: Question word
Asks about
Example
rows: the way, what it is like
a price, an amount, a number

blocks.text: *¿Por qué?* asks why: two words with an accent. *Porque* answers: one word, no accent. *¿Por qué estudias español? Porque vivo aquí.* *Cuánto* agrees with its noun: *¿Cuántos años tienes? ¿Cuánta leche quieres?*
Negatives with no
Put *no* right before the verb. In a short answer you often hear it twice: the first *no* answers, the second makes the verb negative: *¿Trabajas hoy? No, no trabajo.*
Two negative words are correct
After the verb, Spanish uses a second negative word: *No tengo nada.* If the negative word comes before the verb, *no* goes away: *Nunca como carne. Nadie sabe.*
In English, two negatives cancel each other out. In Spanish they don't: with *no* before the verb, use *nada*, *nadie* or *nunca*.

comic: Stop! Problema is masculine: el problema.

blocks.text: Every Spanish noun is masculine or feminine, also words for things. Articles and adjectives change to match the noun: *el piso pequeño, la casa pequeña, los pisos pequeños, las casas pequeñas*.
Masculine or feminine?
The ending of a noun usually tells you. For other endings, learn the word together with its article.

head: Ending
Usually
Examples
rows: el libro, el piso, el médico
la casa, la mesa, la médica
la información, la habitación, la ciudad
el coche, la calle, el hospital, la luz

blocks.text: Common exceptions: *el día, el problema, el idioma, el mapa* are masculine; *la mano, la foto, la moto* are feminine. Feminine nouns with a stressed *a-* at the start take *el* in the singular: *el agua fría* (but *las aguas*).
Articles

Spanish uses *el, la, los, las* also for things in general, where English has no article: *Me gusta el café. Los niños juegan mucho.* It uses no *un* or *una* for a plain job after *ser*, or for things people normally have one of: *Es médica. Tengo coche.*
*a* + *el* = *al*, and *de* + *el* = *del*: *Voy al médico. Vengo del trabajo.* Not with *la*: *Voy a la farmacia.*
Plurals

head: Rule
Singular → plural
rows: the written accent can go or come

blocks.text: Adjectives
An adjective usually goes after the noun and agrees with it. For a mixed group of men and women, use the masculine plural: *Mis hijos son altos* can mean sons and daughters.

head: Adjective ends in
Masculine
Feminine
rows: el piso nuevo, los pisos nuevos
la casa nueva, las casas nuevas
el coche grande, los coches grandes
la casa grande, las casas grandes
el libro fácil, los libros fáciles
la clase fácil, las clases fáciles

blocks.text: hay or está?
*Hay* means “there is” and “there are”, and it has only this one form. Use it for new information, with *un, una*, a number or no article. For a known, particular thing, use *está* or *están*.

head: hay
está / están
rows: La farmacia está en la plaza.
En mi calle hay dos bares.

blocks.text: *Coche* is masculine, so the article and the adjective are masculine too. A noun in *-e* doesn't show its gender: learn it with the article.

B. Write the plural.

blocks.text: The most common Spanish verbs are irregular. The good news: there are only a few patterns, and the endings stay almost the same as in Chapter 2.
Four verbs to learn first
*Tener* is for age, hunger and more, where English uses “be”: *Tengo 31 años. Tengo hambre. Tengo frío.* *Ir* goes with *a*: *Voy a Madrid. Vamos al médico.*
Irregular only in the yo form
Some verbs are irregular only with *yo*. All the other persons are regular.

head: Verb
yo
tú
Example
rows: Veo la tele por la noche.

blocks.text: *Saber* is to know a fact or how to do something: *Sé conducir.* *Conocer* is to know a person or a place: *Conozco Sevilla. Conozco a Lucía.* A person needs *a* after the verb.
Stem-changing verbs
In these verbs a vowel in the stem changes in every form except *nosotros* and *vosotros*. The endings are normal.
e → ie: empezar, cerrar, entender, pensar, preferir · o → ue: volver, dormir, costar, encontrar · e → i: repetir, servir

items: ¿Puedo pagar con tarjeta? Sí, claro.
La oficina cierra a las dos.
Vengo de la oficina y voy al médico.
No entiendo esta carta. ¿Me ayudas?
Hago la compra los sábados.

blocks.text: *Saber* is irregular with *yo*: *sé*. Learn the *yo* form together with the verb: *sé, hago, tengo, salgo*.

chapters.titleDe: Gustar, reflexive verbs and object pronouns

es419.note: Spain also accepts le for a man as direct object (Le veo); Latin America prefers lo (Lo veo). Lo is right everywhere.

comic: Stop! The coffee pleases you: me gusta.

blocks.text: Spanish has small pronouns (*me, te, lo, la, le, se…*) that usually go right before the verb. This chapter shows the three patterns you use every day.
gustar: what you like

With *gustar*, the thing you like is the subject: *Me gusta el café* means “coffee pleases me”. So the verb agrees with the thing: *gusta* for one thing or a verb, *gustan* for more than one thing. The words *a mí, a ti…* are extra, for emphasis or contrast.

head: For emphasis
One thing or a verb
More than one thing
rows: a él / a ella / a usted
a ellos / a ellas / a ustedes

blocks.text: To agree: *Me gusta el café. A mí también.* / *No me gusta el café. A mí tampoco.* Verbs like *encantar* and *doler* work the same way: *Me encantan las tapas. Me duele la cabeza.*
Reflexive verbs
These verbs have *se* at the end in the dictionary: *levantarse*. The pronoun changes with the person and goes before the verb. Many of them describe your daily routine.
levantarse · ducharse · vestirse · acostarse · llamarse · irse · quedarse · sentirse
With an infinitive, the pronoun can go on the end of it or before the first verb. Both are right: *Quiero ducharme. Me quiero duchar.*

items: Me levanto a las seis y media.
¿Cómo se llama usted?
Los niños se acuestan a las nueve.
Hoy me quedo en casa.

blocks.text: Object pronouns
An object pronoun replaces a person or a thing. A direct object answers “what?” or “who?”. An indirect object answers “to whom?”. Only the third person has different forms.

items: ¿Tienes las llaves? Sí, las tengo.
¿Ves a Carmen? Sí, la veo.
Le escribo un correo a mi jefa.
¿Me ayudas? Te llamo esta tarde.

blocks.text: A person as direct object takes *a*: *Veo a Ana.* (a thing doesn't: *Veo la casa*). With two pronouns, the indirect one comes first, and *le* or *les* becomes *se*: *Se lo doy.* In Spain you may also hear *Le veo* for a man; *Lo veo* is always right.
With more than one thing, use *gustan*. The verb agrees with what you like, not with the person.

chapters.titleDe: Two verbs together: tener que, poder, ir a, estar + gerund
comic: Stop! Something you have to do: tener que.

blocks.text: Many everyday meanings come from two verbs together. Only the first verb changes; the second stays an infinitive or a gerund.
Verb + infinitive

head: Verb
Meaning
Example
rows: have to: you or someone in particular
you have to: a rule for everybody

blocks.text: The first verb takes the ending for the person; the infinitive never changes. *Hay que* has only this one form.

*No tienes que venir* = it isn't necessary. *No debes venir* = you shouldn't come. *No puedes venir* = you can't, or you aren't allowed. And *Sé conducir* = I know how; *Hoy no puedo conducir* = today I can't.
ir a + infinitive: the near future
This is the most common way to talk about plans. Use the present of *ir*, then *a*, then the infinitive.
esta tarde · esta noche · mañana · la semana que viene · el mes que viene · el año que viene
estar + gerund: what is happening right now

head: Rule
Examples
rows: -ir verbs with a stem change: e → i, o → u
pedir → pidiendo, decir → diciendo, dormir → durmiendo

blocks.text: Spanish uses this for the moment of speaking, not for the future: *Mañana trabajo* or *Mañana voy a trabajar*, not *Mañana estoy trabajando*. With *ir* and *venir*, use the normal present: *¿Adónde vas?*

items: Tenemos que llevar el pasaporte y el padrón.
Hay que pagar antes de entrar.
Hoy no puedo ir porque estoy enfermo.
Mi hija va a empezar el colegio en septiembre.
¿Qué estás haciendo? Estoy buscando las llaves.

blocks.text: After *hay que, tener que, poder, querer* and *ir a*, the second verb stays in the infinitive.

chapters.titleDe: Talking about the past: perfecto and indefinido

es419.note: In most of Latin America the indefinido is also normal for today and recent events: Hoy comí tarde.

comic: Stop! Ayer is finished time: in Spain, use fui.

blocks.text: In Spain, two past tenses tell you what happened. The *pretérito perfecto* (*he comido*) is for time that is not finished. The *pretérito indefinido* (*comí*) is for finished time.
Pretérito perfecto: haber + participle
The participle ends in *-ado* (*-ar* verbs) or *-ido* (*-er* and *-ir* verbs). It never changes, and nothing goes between it and *haber*: *No he comido.*

blocks.title: Irregular participles
head: Verb
Participle
Verb
Participle

blocks.text: In Spain it goes with time words for time that is still going on, and with *ya, todavía no* and *nunca*: *Hoy he comido tarde. ¿Ya has pedido cita? Todavía no.* In much of Latin America people prefer the *indefinido* here: *Hoy comí tarde.*
Pretérito indefinido: regular verbs
The accent decides: *hablo* = I speak, *habló* = he or she spoke. Verbs in *-car, -gar, -zar* change their spelling with *yo*: *busqué, llegué, empecé*.
Common irregular verbs
These irregular forms have no written accent: *tuve, hizo, fui*. *Ser* and *ir* share their forms; the sentence tells you which one it is: *Fue médica. Fue al médico.*
Which one do I use?

When the time is finished (*ayer, el lunes, la semana pasada, en 2019, hace dos días*), use the *indefinido*. When the time is not finished (*hoy, esta semana, este año*) or you talk about experience up to now (*alguna vez, nunca, ya, todavía no*), use the *perfecto*.

head: perfecto
indefinido
rows: Esta semana he ido al médico.
La semana pasada fui al médico.
Todavía no he recibido la carta.
Recibí la carta hace dos días.

items: ¿Has comido ya? Sí, ya he comido.
Llegué a España en 2021.
Ayer fui al ayuntamiento y pedí cita.
Este año hemos cambiado de piso.
¿Qué hiciste el fin de semana? Fui a la playa con mis hijos.

blocks.text: *Ayer* is finished time, so in Spain you use the *indefinido*.

chapters.titleDe: The imperfecto and telling a story
comic: Stop! The time is background: use the imperfecto.

blocks.text: The *imperfecto* describes the past: what things were like, what was going on, what used to happen. Together with the *indefinido*, which says what happened next, it lets you tell a story.
The forms
*-ar* verbs take *-aba*, and *-er* and *-ir* verbs take *-ía*. The *yo* and *él* forms are the same. Only three verbs are irregular: *ser, ir* and *ver*.

blocks.title: The three irregular verbs
head: Person
ser
ir
ver

blocks.text: When do we use it?

head: Use
Example
rows: a habit, what used to happen
De niño jugaba en la calle.
La casa era pequeña y tenía un patio.
age, time and weather in the past
Tenía 20 años. Eran las ocho y hacía frío.
an action that was going on

blocks.text: antes · de niño / de niña · siempre · todos los días · a menudo · cuando era joven · mientras
*Antes* + *imperfecto* is the usual way to say “used to”: *Antes vivía en Rumanía; ahora vivo en Castellón.*
Indefinido or imperfecto?
Think of a film. The *imperfecto* is the background: the scene and the situation. The *indefinido* gives the events that move the story on.
A finished period with a clear length takes the *indefinido*: *Viví diez años en Rabat* (and then I left). Compare: *Vivía en Rabat cuando conocí a mi marido.*

blocks.title: A short story
items: Cuando llegué a España, tenía 22 años y no hablaba español.
Vivía con mi prima en un piso pequeño.
Un día vi un anuncio en una panadería, entré y pregunté por el trabajo.
La dueña era muy amable y me dio el trabajo.

blocks.wrong: Cuando tuve 20 años, vine a España.
blocks.right: Cuando tenía 20 años, vine a España.
blocks.text: Your age in the past is background, so it takes the *imperfecto*.

chapters.titleDe: B1 toolkit: future, conditional, si, first subjunctive
comic: Stop! After cuando, a future time takes the subjunctive.

blocks.text: This chapter brings together four things you need at B1: the *futuro*, the *condicional*, sentences with *si*, and your first steps with the *subjuntivo*. Each section shows the basic form; there is more practice online.
Futuro simple
Add the endings to the whole infinitive; all verbs have the same endings. Use it for predictions, promises and plans further away. For near plans, people usually say *ir a* + infinitive (Chapter 7).

blocks.title: Irregular stems (the endings don't change)
head: Verb
Stem
Verb
Stem

blocks.text: Condicional simple
It has the same stems as the *futuro*, with the endings *-ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -íais, -ían*: *hablaría, viviría, tendría, haría*. Use it to sound polite and to imagine something.

head: Use
Example
rows: Me gustaría hablar con la directora.
Yo que tú, hablaría con el casero. Deberías descansar.

blocks.text: si: real conditions
*Si* + present, then a present, a future or an imperative. Use this for things that can really happen. When the *si* part comes first, put a comma after it.
There is no *futuro* and no present subjunctive right after *si*: *Si tengo tiempo, te llamaré*, not *Si tendré tiempo*. Imagined conditions (*Si tuviera…*) come at B2.
Your first subjunctive
Start from the *yo* form of the present and swap the vowel: *-ar* verbs take *e*, *-er* and *-ir* verbs take *a*: *hablo → hable, como → coma, tengo → tenga, hago → haga*.
Irregular: ser → sea · ir → vaya · estar → esté · haber → haya · saber → sepa · dar → dé

head: When
Example
rows: a wish for someone else: quiero que, espero que
Quiero que vengas. Espero que estés bien.
a future time: cuando, en cuanto, hasta que
Te lo explico para que lo entiendas.

blocks.text: Same person: infinitive. *Quiero ir.* Different person: *que* + subjunctive. *Quiero que vayas.* After *creo que*, use the normal present: *Creo que viene.* For a habit, *cuando* also takes the normal present: *Cuando llego a casa, cocino.*

items: El mes que viene empezaré un curso.
¿Me podría decir dónde está la oficina?
Si necesitas ayuda, llámame.
Espero que encuentres trabajo pronto.
Cuando tenga los papeles, buscaré un piso.

blocks.text: Right after *si*, use the present, even when you mean the future.

blocks.title: A. Write the verb in the futuro.

items.q: El año que viene yo ___ (tener) más tiempo.

blocks.title: B. Write the verb in the condicional.

items.q: Nosotros ___ (comprar) ese piso, pero es muy caro.

blocks.title: C. Write the verb after si.

items.q: Si yo ___ (perder) el autobús, llegaré tarde.

es419.note: Vosotros form; Latin America uses ustedes estudian.

blocks.title: D. Subjunctive, normal present or infinitive? Write the correct form.

items.q: Cuando tú ___ (llegar) a casa mañana, llámame.
Cuando yo ___ (llegar) a casa, siempre cocino.
